cards.title: Kubernetes in 2026: The Frontier
cards.teaser: Kubernetes turns twelve in 2026 and the control-plane primitives are stable — but the platform is no longer just about containers. WASM runtimes, eBPF dataplanes, GPU scheduling, and AI-augmented orchestration are reshaping what it means to run workloads on K8s.

runs.text: Note: this chapter is a snapshot, not a forecast. The K8s ecosystem moves fast enough that specific projects cited here may be superseded within the 9-month refresh window. Underlying engineering problems are designed to outlast the examples.
The structural shape of Kubernetes — declarative desired state, reconciliation loops, extensible APIs — has not changed since the 1.0 release in 2015. What has changed is
what runs on it and how
. Several concurrent shifts define the 2026 landscape:

items.text: Alternative workload types.

WebAssembly (WASM) modules run alongside OCI containers on the same nodes through containerd's runwasi integration. GPU pods and accelerator-attached workloads are first-class scheduling targets. The container is no longer the only workload unit.
Dataplane reinvention.
eBPF-based networking (Cilium, Isovalent) has replaced kube-proxy in a growing majority of new production deployments. Kernel programmability removes the need for iptables chains entirely.
Policy as code, not webhooks.
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL expressions reduced the webhook sprawl that plagued clusters in 2021-2023. Gateway API graduated, replacing Ingress as the canonical traffic model.
AI-in-the-loop.

Experimental schedulers and capacity planners use ML models to predict resource demand and pre-provision nodes. This is research-grade in 2026 but approaching proof-of-concept at scale at a handful of hyperscalers.

runs.text: The CNCF Annual Survey 2025 reported that Kubernetes adoption has plateaued in breadth (most organisations who will adopt it already have) but is accelerating in depth — more workload types, more clusters per org, more custom extensions. The challenge has shifted from 'how do we get started' to 'how do we operate at scale'.

Kubernetes' core idea — declare what you want, let reconciliation loops make it happen — hasn't changed. What has changed is what you can run on it: WASM modules, GPU workloads, and AI-driven scheduling are expanding the platform well beyond OCI containers.

cards.title: WASM Workloads: The Container Alternative
cards.teaser: WebAssembly modules start in milliseconds, run in a sandboxed environment, and are orders of magnitude smaller than container images. The engineering question in 2026 is not whether WASM belongs on Kubernetes — it does — but which runtime model is ready for production.

runs.text: WebAssembly (WASM) was designed for the browser but its security and portability properties make it a compelling alternative to containers for certain server-side workloads. A WASM module is a compact binary that can execute in a sandboxed environment with no OS dependency — the same binary runs on x86, ARM, or RISC-V without modification. Startup latency is sub-millisecond, compared to tens of milliseconds for a container with a full Linux userspace.
The engineering problems WASM solves better than containers:

items.text: Cold start latency.

A WASM module starts in under 1ms. A minimal container (Alpine + single binary) is 10-50ms. A full JVM-based container can be 2-10 seconds. For functions-as-a-service patterns, WASM's cold start is unmatched.
Image size.
A WASM module compiled from Rust or Go is typically 1-10 MB, versus 50-300 MB for an equivalent container image. This matters at the edge and in environments with constrained pull bandwidth.
Sandboxing model.

WASM's capability-based sandboxing (via WASI — the WebAssembly System Interface) grants only the system access explicitly requested. A WASM module that doesn't declare filesystem access can't touch the filesystem — the sandbox is enforced by the runtime, not by Linux cgroups and seccomp profiles.

runs.text: Where WASM still lags containers in 2026:

items.text: Language support is uneven.
Rust, Go (via TinyGo), and C/C++ compile well to WASM. Python, Java, and Ruby can run inside WASM runtimes but with significant overhead — the interpreter itself runs in WASM.
Networking and I/O are immature.
WASI's socket support (wasi-sockets) was in preview in 2025. Production HTTP workloads require frameworks like Spin (Fermyon) that abstract the networking layer.
Ecosystem tooling is young.
Observability, debugging, and profiling for WASM workloads on Kubernetes are significantly less mature than for containers.

runs.text: ByteDance reported running WASM workloads in production on Kubernetes in 2024, citing the cold-start advantage for their event-driven processing. Shopify has used WASM (via its Liquid/Hydrogen product extension system) for plugin sandboxing since 2022. These are greenfield deployments, not container migrations.

WASM modules are tiny, start in under 1ms, and run in a capability-based sandbox — making them a better fit than containers for cold-start-sensitive workloads. The limitation in 2026 is ecosystem maturity: language support and networking are still catching up to the container world.

cards.title: SpinKube, runwasi, and WASM on K8s
cards.teaser: Getting WASM modules to run on Kubernetes requires either a purpose-built runtime shim or a WASM-aware containerd integration. SpinKube and runwasi take different approaches — and both are converging on the same containerd shim architecture.

runs.text: The Kubernetes runtime interface (CRI) expects workloads in OCI container format. Running WASM natively requires bridging between the CRI and a WASM runtime. Two integration strategies have emerged:

items.text: runwasi.

A containerd shim project (CNCF sandbox, 2023) that allows containerd to run WASM workloads directly using Wasmtime or WASMedge as the underlying runtime. When containerd receives an OCI image whose annotation indicates it contains a WASM module (the
module.wasm.image/variant: compat

convention), it routes execution to the appropriate runwasi shim rather than to runc. This is transparent to the scheduler — Kubernetes sees a normal pod; the node decides at execution time how to run it.
SpinKube.

A higher-level CNCF project (Sandbox, 2024) built by Fermyon, Microsoft, and Liquid Reply. SpinKube provides a SpinApp CRD and an operator that manages the lifecycle of Spin-based WASM applications on Kubernetes. It handles distributing WASM binaries as OCI artifacts, configuring the containerd-wasm-shim, and exposing service endpoints. SpinKube is the production-ready abstraction for teams who want to run Fermyon Spin apps on K8s without building their own operator.
Krustlet (deprecated).

The original WASM-on-K8s approach from Deis/Microsoft (2019-2022): a virtual kubelet implemented in Rust that registered as a K8s node and ran WASM modules directly. Krustlet was archived in 2022 when the runwasi / containerd-shim approach proved more operationally tractable. It is mentioned here because many blog posts still reference it — do not build on Krustlet.

runs.text: The containerd-shim architecture (runwasi's approach) is the winning pattern because it re-uses the existing K8s scheduling, resource model, and observability pipeline — the WASM runtime is just a different execution backend at the node level. No separate node pools, no custom kubelet forks.
Practical deployment (2026): annotate the node pool with a runtime class, define a
RuntimeClass
referencing the wasm shim handler, and specify that RuntimeClass in pod specs. Mixed-runtime clusters (some pods as OCI containers, some as WASM modules) are fully supported.

WASM workloads on K8s are production-viable in 2026 for stateless HTTP handlers and event processors written in Rust or Go. They are not viable for anything requiring POSIX threading, direct GPU access, or large language runtimes (Python/JVM). Match the runtime to the workload profile.

runwasi is a containerd shim that routes WASM-annotated OCI images to a WASM runtime instead of runc. SpinKube is a higher-level operator that manages Spin WASM apps on K8s. Both use the same K8s scheduling and observability machinery — only the last-mile execution changes.

cards.title: eBPF Dataplanes: Beyond kube-proxy
cards.teaser: eBPF lets you run verified programs in the Linux kernel without kernel modules. Cilium uses this to replace kube-proxy's iptables chains with kernel-native BPF maps — delivering lower latency, better observability, and network policy enforcement that containers cannot bypass.

runs.text: kube-proxy has been Kubernetes' default service proxy since 1.0. It maintains iptables rules (or IPVS entries) that translate ClusterIP service addresses to pod IPs. The problem at scale: iptables is a sequential chain — adding a rule means traversing all preceding rules on every packet. A cluster with 10,000 services and 50,000 pods can have hundreds of thousands of iptables rules, and rule traversal adds measurable per-packet latency.

eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) solves this at the kernel level. An eBPF program is a restricted, safely-typed bytecode that is JIT-compiled and loaded into the kernel at specific hook points (packet ingress/egress, socket syscalls, tracepoints). The kernel verifier guarantees the program terminates and cannot corrupt kernel memory. This is not a userspace proxy — the program executes directly in the network stack, before packets reach userspace.
Cilium's eBPF-native implementation:

items.text: kube-proxy replacement.

Cilium's BPF-based load balancer uses a hash map for O(1) service IP lookup instead of O(n) iptables chain traversal. At 10,000 services, eBPF lookup is constant time; iptables traversal grows linearly.
Network policy enforcement.

NetworkPolicy rules are compiled into BPF programs attached to each pod's veth interface. Because enforcement happens in the kernel before the packet reaches the container, a compromised container cannot bypass policy by manipulating iptables.
Deep observability without sidecars.

Cilium Hubble captures L3/L4/L7 flow data (HTTP method, gRPC status, DNS queries) from BPF hooks without injecting a sidecar proxy into every pod. This is the core advantage over service meshes for observability: no per-pod CPU/memory overhead.
Bandwidth management.
eBPF-based EDT (Earliest Departure Time) rate limiting replaces tc-based bandwidth limiting with a more precise and lower-overhead mechanism.

runs.text: Adoption signal: Cilium is the default CNI on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE Dataplane V2, since 2021), AWS EKS's VPC CNI in eBPF mode (2023), and is used by Adobe, Capital One, and most large Kubernetes deployments started after 2022. The Cilium project graduated from CNCF in 2023.

eBPF is the most significant low-level infrastructure shift in Linux networking since iptables replaced ipchains in 2001. It is not a Kubernetes-specific technology — it also underlies Meta's Katran load balancer, Cloudflare's DDoS mitigation, and Linux kernel observability tools like bpftrace. Understanding eBPF's kernel hook model is increasingly a prerequisite for senior platform engineering roles.

eBPF lets Cilium replace kube-proxy's iptables chains with kernel-native hash maps, making service lookup O(1) instead of O(n). It also enforces network policy in the kernel, where containers can't bypass it, and captures detailed flow telemetry without sidecar proxies.

cards.title: AI-Augmented Scheduling
cards.teaser: The default Kubernetes scheduler is deterministic and stateless — it sees one pod at a time and makes placement decisions from static resource requests. ML-driven schedulers attempt to learn cluster-wide demand patterns and pre-place workloads before the load arrives. This is still emerging in 2026.

runs.text: Note: AI-augmented scheduling is explicitly speculative as of 2026. The production-proven tier is thin; the research-and-internal-tooling tier is substantial. Frame adoption decisions against proven cluster autoscaler solutions before reaching for ML approaches.

The problem the default scheduler does not solve: it optimises each pod placement independently, has no model of historical demand, and makes no predictions. When a batch ML training job arrives, the scheduler bins-packs it into available nodes — but does not anticipate that the same job will arrive every day at 2am and could have nodes pre-provisioned and warmed.
Approaches that have emerged:

items.text: Predictive cluster autoscaling.

KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) combined with time-series forecasting scales node pools proactively based on predicted load. This is proven — not AI scheduling per se, but ML-informed capacity management.
Topology-aware placement.

Kubernetes 1.26+ Topology Spread Constraints and the Descheduler project allow post-hoc rebalancing. These are heuristic, not ML-driven, but address the placement correctness problem that motivates AI scheduling research.
Scheduler extenders and plugins (Volcano).

Volcano (CNCF Incubating) is a batch scheduling framework for ML/HPC workloads that adds gang scheduling, queue management, and resource fairness. It extends the default scheduler rather than replacing it. ByteDance uses Volcano at scale for their ML training infrastructure.
LLM-assisted manifest generation.

A practical near-term application: using an LLM to generate resource requests and limits by analyzing historical pod metrics — closing the gap between under-requested and over-requested pods. Goldilocks (FairwindsOps) and VPA's recommender fulfill a similar role without an LLM.

runs.text: What is genuinely speculative: end-to-end ML schedulers that replace the K8s scheduler with a learned policy network. Academic work exists (DeepRM, Decima from Harvard/CMU, 2016-2019), and internal tooling at Google, Microsoft, and Alibaba is referenced in research papers, but no open-source production-grade ML scheduler for K8s exists as of 2026.

Evaluate AI scheduling claims by asking: does this improve bin-packing efficiency, reduce tail latency, or lower cost — and by how much versus KEDA + VPA + Descheduler? The baseline is already strong. Replacing a well-understood deterministic scheduler with an ML model introduces explainability and debugging complexity that requires a measurable payoff to justify.

AI scheduling means using ML to predict resource demand and place pods proactively instead of reactively. In 2026 this is mostly research and internal hyperscaler tooling. The practical equivalent — KEDA for event-driven autoscaling and VPA for resource recommendations — is proven and widely deployed.

cards.title: Serverless K8s: Knative and KEDA
cards.teaser: Scale-to-zero is the defining serverless property: when no requests are in flight, compute drops to zero; when a request arrives, a pod starts. Knative and KEDA deliver this on top of standard K8s — Knative for HTTP workloads, KEDA for event-driven scaling from any source.

runs.text: The problem serverless-on-K8s solves: provisioned Deployments waste compute when idle. A microservice handling 1 request per hour still holds its CPU reservation 24/7. For batch processors, event consumers, and low-traffic services, this waste accumulates across hundreds of services in a mature platform.
Knative Serving (CNCF Incubating, Google-led) adds HTTP-triggered scale-to-zero to Kubernetes:

items.text: Request queuing during scale-up.
The Knative activator buffers incoming requests while a pod starts. Cold start is bounded by container startup time — WASM shims on Knative bring this to sub-100ms for appropriate workloads.
Revision-based traffic splitting.
Knative's Route object allows percentage-based traffic splits across revisions (versions) of a service — enabling canary deployments and A/B testing without an external ingress controller feature.
Concurrency-based autoscaling.
Knative's autoscaler scales on concurrent requests per pod (KPA) rather than CPU utilization, which is a better signal for latency-sensitive HTTP handlers.

runs.text: KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling, CNCF Graduated 2023) extends HPA to scale on any external metric source — not just CPU/memory:

items.text: Scalers for 60+ sources.

Kafka consumer lag, SQS queue depth, Redis list length, Prometheus query results, Azure Service Bus message count, GitHub Actions queue — KEDA can scale a Deployment to zero when the queue is empty and to N replicas per queue item.
Scale to zero for Jobs.
KEDA's ScaledJob object creates K8s Jobs on demand per event — one Job per message, with configurable parallelism and backoff. This is the idiomatic pattern for batch processing workloads.
HTTP add-on.
The KEDA HTTP Add-on provides Knative-style HTTP scale-to-zero without requiring Knative Serving, trading Knative's revision model for simpler KEDA-native configuration.

runs.text: Knative and KEDA address different root problems. Knative's strength is HTTP traffic management and revision-based canaries; its weakness is operational complexity (it requires Istio or Kourier as a networking layer). KEDA's strength is breadth of event sources and simplicity; it does not provide traffic splitting. Many platforms deploy both: KEDA for queue-driven workloads, Knative (or a simpler HTTP trigger) for latency-sensitive HTTP handlers.

Knative adds HTTP scale-to-zero with request buffering and revision-based traffic splits. KEDA scales workloads from any event source — Kafka lag, SQS depth, Prometheus queries — including to zero. Together they cover most serverless-on-K8s patterns without leaving the Kubernetes API.

cards.title: Multi-Tenancy: vCluster and Capsule
cards.teaser: Hard multi-tenancy on a single Kubernetes cluster remains unsolved at the API level. vCluster and Capsule take opposite approaches: vCluster gives each tenant a full virtual cluster; Capsule enforces tenant boundaries within the same control plane using namespace grouping and policy.

runs.text: Kubernetes was not designed for multi-tenancy. A namespace provides resource naming isolation but shares the control plane, the API server, and the underlying nodes. A tenant with Deployment/create access can theoretically exhaust the cluster's scheduling capacity. A misconfigured ClusterRole can expose secrets across namespaces. The failure mode is not theoretical — it has caused incidents at public cloud providers.
The spectrum from soft to hard multi-tenancy:

items.text: Soft multi-tenancy (namespaces + RBAC + ResourceQuota).

Appropriate when all tenants are trusted internal teams. Namespace boundaries prevent naming collision; RBAC restricts API access per tenant; ResourceQuota caps resource consumption. Does not provide kernel isolation — a container escape on one tenant's pod affects all tenants on the node.
Capsule (namespace-as-tenant, Clastix).

A CNCF Sandbox project that groups multiple namespaces into a Tenant object. A tenant admin can create namespaces within their Tenant but cannot see or affect other Tenants. Capsule uses a ValidatingWebhook (being migrated to ValidatingAdmissionPolicy) to enforce policies across all tenant namespaces. Good fit for internal platform teams offering self-service namespace creation with guardrails.
vCluster (Loft Labs).

Creates a virtual Kubernetes cluster as a StatefulSet inside a host namespace. Each virtual cluster runs its own API server (k3s or k8s) and syncs selected resources to the host cluster. Tenants get a full K8s API surface — CRDs, ClusterRoles, their own admission webhooks — without sharing the host control plane. Used heavily for CI environments (ephemeral clusters per PR), developer sandboxes, and SaaS products shipping 'managed K8s' to customers.
Separate clusters.

The only true hard multi-tenancy. Expensive in control plane cost but eliminates shared-fate scenarios entirely. The operational overhead is addressed by cluster fleet management tools (Cluster API, Argo CD App of Apps).

runs.text: Decision heuristic: if tenants are mutually trusting teams, Capsule. If tenants need full K8s API access (their own CRDs, their own admission webhooks), vCluster. If tenants include untrusted external customers or security blast radius is unacceptable, separate clusters with Cluster API.

vCluster's virtual control plane runs in the host cluster. A misconfigured sync rule can expose host cluster resources to virtual cluster tenants. Review the syncer configuration carefully — the default sync-up rules for nodes and persistent volumes can over-expose host infrastructure if not scoped correctly.

Capsule groups namespaces into Tenants on a shared cluster — good for internal teams. vCluster gives each tenant a full virtual cluster running as a pod — good when tenants need their own CRDs or webhooks. Separate clusters give true isolation but cost more to operate.

cards.title: GPU and Accelerator Scheduling
cards.teaser: Running GPU workloads on Kubernetes requires the NVIDIA device plugin, a runtime that exposes GPU devices to containers, and scheduling policies that prevent GPU fragmentation. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) and time-slicing add flexibility — and operational complexity.

runs.text: As ML inference and training workloads move to Kubernetes, GPU scheduling has become a first-class concern. The default K8s resource model (integer CPU/memory) does not map well to GPU resources — a single A100 GPU is worth tens of thousands of dollars and can often serve multiple smaller workloads concurrently.
The NVIDIA GPU stack on Kubernetes:

items.text: NVIDIA Device Plugin.
A DaemonSet that discovers GPUs on each node and advertises them as schedulable resources (
nvidia.com/gpu: 1
). Pods request GPUs in resource limits. Without this plugin, containers cannot access GPU devices. Required for any CUDA-dependent workload.
NVIDIA Container Runtime.

Wraps runc to inject NVIDIA driver mounts and device bindings into the container before it starts. Configured as an OCI runtime hook or as a containerd runtime class. Without it, the GPU device node is visible but CUDA initialization fails.
MIG (Multi-Instance GPU, Ampere and later).

Hardware partitioning that divides a single A100 into up to 7 independent instances, each with its own memory and compute slice. MIG instances appear as separate schedulable resources to Kubernetes. Enables multiple inference workloads to share one physical GPU with true hardware isolation — not time-slicing.
Time-slicing and MPS.

For GPUs that predate Ampere (no MIG support), the NVIDIA device plugin supports time-slicing — advertising a GPU as N virtual GPUs that share time. NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) provides a similar effect with lower context-switch overhead. Both lack the hardware isolation of MIG.

runs.text: Beyond NVIDIA: AMD ROCm and Intel Gaudi (formerly Habana Labs) are gaining Kubernetes support through device plugins. The Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) API (see card 12) was motivated in part by the limitations of the integer GPU resource model — DRA enables richer allocation semantics like 'any 2 GPUs on the same PCIe switch'.

GPU fragmentation — the problem where large integer GPU requests can't fit on any node even though aggregate cluster capacity is sufficient — is a real operational headache. Volcano's gang scheduling and the NVIDIA GPU Operator's bin-packing scheduler plugin both address this. Monitor GPU utilization per node; consistently low utilization on a node with pending GPU pods is the fragmentation signal.

The NVIDIA device plugin tells Kubernetes about GPUs; the NVIDIA container runtime injects CUDA drivers into pods. MIG slices a single A100 into up to 7 hardware-isolated instances. Time-slicing and MPS let multiple pods share a GPU without MIG, but without hardware isolation.

cards.title: ARM and Multi-Arch Clusters
cards.teaser: AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon (M-series), and Ampere Altra have made ARM a first-class server architecture. Multi-arch clusters run mixed x86 and ARM nodes — reducing cost by 20-40% on ARM-eligible workloads — but require multi-arch container images and careful build matrix design.

runs.text: The economic argument for ARM on Kubernetes is clear: AWS Graviton3 instances deliver roughly the same throughput as equivalent x86 instances at 20-40% lower cost per core, with better performance per watt. AWS EKS, GKE, and AKS all support ARM node pools. Teams with mature container platforms are running mixed clusters where ARM-eligible workloads (stateless HTTP services, caches) run on ARM nodes and x86-only workloads (legacy binaries, certain ML kernels) run on x86 nodes.
The infrastructure requirements for multi-arch clusters:

items.text: Multi-arch image manifests.
An OCI image index (manifest list) references multiple image variants by architecture. When containerd pulls
myapp:latest
on an ARM node, it selects the arm64 variant automatically. Building these requires Docker Buildx or equivalent with QEMU cross-compilation or native ARM build runners.
CI build matrices.
The most reliable multi-arch build strategy is native compilation: run separate build jobs on x86 and ARM runners, then combine the manifests with
docker manifest create
or
crane
. QEMU emulation is slower (5-10x) and can miss architecture-specific compilation failures.
Node affinity and taints.
Workloads that are not yet multi-arch need node affinity rules to prevent scheduling on ARM nodes. Use kubernetes.io/arch labels:
nodeAffinity: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: nodeSelectorTerms: [{matchExpressions: [{key: kubernetes.io/arch, operator: In, values: [amd64]}]}]
Base image parity.

Verify that all base images in Dockerfiles have multi-arch variants. Older third-party images frequently have only amd64 variants. This is the most common operational surprise when starting multi-arch adoption.

runs.text: Local development on Apple Silicon (M-series Macs) is a forcing function: engineers who build containers on M1/M2/M3 and push to x86 clusters regularly hit this problem. The correct solution is multi-arch images, not arm64 → amd64 QEMU translation on CI.

Graviton4 (r8g instances, 2024) extended Graviton's advantage to memory-intensive workloads. The cost-performance case for ARM is strong enough that new Kubernetes platforms started in 2025 should default to ARM-first with x86 as the exception, not the other way around.

Multi-arch clusters run ARM and x86 nodes together. ARM saves 20-40% on compute costs. The prerequisite is multi-arch OCI image manifests — one image tag that pulls the right variant per architecture. The build challenge is making CI produce native-compiled images for both architectures.

cards.title: Confidential Containers and TEEs
cards.teaser: Confidential containers run inside a hardware-backed Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) — Intel TDX, AMD SEV, or ARM CCA — where even the host OS and hypervisor cannot read the workload's memory. This solves a compliance problem that Kubernetes RBAC and encryption at rest cannot.

runs.text: The problem confidential computing solves: in a shared cloud environment, the host operator (cloud provider, hypervisor, cluster admin) has physical access to the hardware and — without TEEs — can read the memory of any running VM or container. For regulated workloads (healthcare data, financial records, cryptographic key material), this is a compliance blocker regardless of contractual assurances.
TEE models:

items.text: Intel TDX (Trust Domain Extensions, Sapphire Rapids 2023+).

Encrypts entire VM memory at the hardware level. The VMM (hypervisor) cannot read the VM's memory. Remote attestation allows the tenant to verify that their workload is running on genuine TDX hardware with an unmodified measurement. Designed for VM-level confidentiality — an entire K8s node can be a trust domain.
AMD SEV-SNP (Secure Encrypted Virtualization, EPYC 3rd gen+).

Similar to TDX: hardware-encrypted VM memory with remote attestation. SEV-SNP (2022) added integrity protection against replay attacks. Available on AWS (m6a, c6a, r6a instances with SEV) and Azure (DCasv5 confidential VMs). Currently the more widely deployed TEE in cloud production.
Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions).

An older TEE model that protects a small enclave of application code and data (EPC, typically 256MB-1GB). The application must be rewritten or ported to use SGX APIs. Much more intrusive than TDX/SEV but has a richer remote attestation ecosystem. Less relevant for K8s workloads due to the porting burden.

runs.text: Confidential Containers on Kubernetes (CNCF Sandbox project, cloud-hypervisor + kata-containers + attestation agent) combines Kata Containers (VM-based container isolation) with a TEE-enabled guest kernel. The pod runs inside an encrypted VM; the kubelet communicates with the guest through a minimal, attestation-verified interface.

Adoption status (2026): confidential containers are in production at regulated financial services and healthcare organizations on Azure (DCasv5) and AWS. They add 5-15% performance overhead (memory encryption) and require hardware attestation infrastructure. Not yet mainstream — consider for workloads where compliance or data sensitivity explicitly requires in-use encryption.

Confidential containers protect workload memory from the host. They do not protect against application vulnerabilities, compromised container images, or malicious code inside the trust domain. Defense in depth still applies — TEEs are a layer in the security model, not a replacement for it.

Confidential containers run inside hardware-encrypted VM memory (Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP) so the cloud provider and host OS cannot read the workload's data. Remote attestation proves the workload is running on genuine hardware. Useful for regulated data where 'trust the cloud provider' is not an acceptable answer.

cards.title: Native Sidecars and CRI Evolution
cards.teaser: Kubernetes 1.30 made sidecar containers a GA first-class concept with ordered startup/shutdown semantics. Meanwhile, the CRI ecosystem has consolidated around containerd and CRI-O, with Kata Containers and gVisor providing hardened runtime alternatives for untrusted workloads.

runs.text: The sidecar problem: in the service mesh era, nearly every pod runs a proxy container (Envoy, Linkerd-proxy) as a sidecar. The original K8s model had no ordering guarantees — the sidecar and the application container started and terminated in undefined order. A sidecar proxy that stopped before the application container could drop in-flight requests; a proxy that started after the application could miss early traffic. Teams worked around this with complex entrypoint scripts and liveness probe hacks.
Native sidecars (KEP-753, Alpha in 1.28, Beta in 1.29, GA in 1.30+):

items.text: Declared via initContainers with restartPolicy: Always.
This turns an init container into a sidecar that stays alive for the pod's lifetime. The scheduler guarantees the sidecar starts and reaches Ready before the main containers start.
Ordered shutdown.
On pod termination, the main containers receive SIGTERM first. Only after all main containers exit does the sidecar receive SIGTERM. This eliminates the proxy-drops-traffic-at-shutdown problem.
Job compatibility.

A Job's completion is now correctly detected even when sidecars are present — the Job completes when the main container exits, not when the sidecar exits. Previously, sidecar-equipped Jobs required manual workarounds.

runs.text: The CRI runtime landscape in 2026:

items.text: containerd (CNCF Graduated).
The default runtime on GKE, EKS, and AKS. Supports pluggable shims (runc, runwasi, Kata, gVisor) via the RuntimeClass API. The consolidation choice for new clusters.
CRI-O.
Red Hat's minimal CRI implementation for OpenShift. No Docker daemon, no extra APIs — strictly the CRI interface plus CNI and OCI. The default on OpenShift clusters.
Kata Containers.

Runs each pod inside a lightweight VM (using firecracker, QEMU, or cloud-hypervisor). The CRI sees a normal pod; the runtime creates a microVM per pod for kernel-level isolation. Used for multi-tenant workloads where container escapes are a realistic threat model.
gVisor (Google).

A user-space kernel (written in Go) that intercepts syscalls from the container and re-implements them in a sandboxed environment. Less overhead than Kata (no full VM) but provides significant isolation against kernel exploit chains. Used on GKE Sandbox.

runs.text: The Docker daemon was removed as a supported K8s runtime in 1.24 (2022). If you are still seeing references to dockershim in documentation, it is outdated. The migration path from dockershim to containerd is complete for all major managed Kubernetes providers.

Native sidecars (GA in K8s 1.30) guarantee that the sidecar starts before and shuts down after the main container — fixing the ordering bugs that plagued service mesh deployments. containerd is the consolidation runtime; Kata Containers and gVisor provide VM-level and user-space-kernel isolation for untrusted workloads.

cards.title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and DRA
cards.teaser: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (GA in 1.30) replaces webhook proliferation with CEL expressions evaluated in the API server. Dynamic Resource Allocation (GA in 1.32) replaces integer-resource device scheduling with a flexible claim model. Both close long-standing Kubernetes extensibility gaps.

runs.text: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP) addresses a real operational problem: as policy-as-code tools (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) proliferated, every cluster accumulated 5-20 admission webhooks. Each webhook is an external network call on every API server write — a latency tax and a reliability dependency. A misbehaving webhook can block all pod creation. VAP moves policy evaluation into the API server itself using Common Expression Language (CEL).
VAP capabilities:

items.text: CEL expressions.
Policies are written as CEL expressions evaluated on the incoming object. Example:
object.spec.replicas <= 10
or
!has(object.metadata.labels) || has(object.metadata.labels.team)
. No webhook, no external call, no availability dependency.
Binding to namespaces.
ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding selects which namespaces and resource types the policy applies to. Policy libraries can be maintained centrally and bound per namespace.
Audit mode.
Policies can be set to Audit (record violations without rejecting) before switching to Deny — the same rollout pattern as Kyverno's audit/enforce modes.

runs.text: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA, KEP-4381, Beta in 1.31, GA in 1.32) replaces the device plugin integer model for allocating complex hardware resources:

items.text: ResourceClaim objects.

Workloads describe what they need from a device (attributes, capacity, topology) rather than requesting an integer count. A ResourceClaim might request 'an NVIDIA GPU with at least 40GB memory on the same PCIe fabric as the requested CPU socket'.
Driver-managed allocation.

The device driver's DRA plugin decides which specific device satisfies the claim, considering topology and sharing constraints. Multiple pods can share a single device claim if the driver supports it.
Structured parameters.

DRA 1.32 added structured parameters that allow the scheduler itself to match claims against device inventory — removing the dependency on a driver webhook for basic scheduling decisions and improving scheduling throughput for large GPU clusters.

runs.text: VAP does not replace Kyverno or Gatekeeper for complex policy scenarios requiring mutation, generate rules, or cross-object lookups. CEL expressions are limited to the admitted object and its namespace context. For simple enforcement (label presence, replica limits, registry allowlists), VAP eliminates the webhook dependency. For complex policy, external tools remain necessary.

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy runs CEL expressions inside the API server instead of calling out to a webhook — eliminating the reliability and latency cost of external admission controllers for simple policies. DRA replaces 'request N GPUs' with a rich claim model that lets drivers allocate devices based on topology, capacity, and sharing constraints.

cards.title: The Post-Docker Era
cards.teaser: Docker Desktop's licensing change in 2022 accelerated a transition that was already underway: the toolchain for building and running containers locally has fragmented into purpose-built alternatives. Rancher Desktop, OrbStack, and Podman Desktop each occupy different niches — and Docker itself remains relevant.

runs.text: Docker's 2022 announcement that Docker Desktop would require a paid subscription for companies over 250 employees or $10M revenue prompted a wave of evaluation of alternatives. The timing coincided with the K8s ecosystem's removal of dockershim (1.24, 2022), closing the 'use Docker in production' path. The result: local container tooling fragmented into a richer ecosystem.
The main alternatives by use case:

items.text: OrbStack (macOS).

A macOS-native VM manager that runs Linux containers and a lightweight K8s cluster with significantly better performance than Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon. OrbStack's networking (no port forwarding required, direct container IPs from the Mac) is its strongest differentiator. By 2025, it is the most common Docker Desktop replacement among macOS developers who benchmark both.
Rancher Desktop (SUSE/Rancher Labs).

Free, open-source desktop tool that bundles containerd (or dockerd in compatibility mode), nerdctl as a Docker-compatible CLI, and a local k3s cluster. The k3s integration makes it the strongest choice for developers who primarily test Kubernetes manifests locally.
Podman Desktop (Red Hat).

A GUI for Podman — the daemonless, rootless container engine that runs containers without a privileged background process. Podman is the default container tool on RHEL/Fedora. Its Docker CLI compatibility layer (
alias docker=podman
) makes migration frictionless for most CLI workflows. Rootless containers (no root daemon) is Podman's security differentiator.
Docker Desktop (Docker Inc.).

Still widely used. The free tier covers individuals and small companies. Its Dev Environments, Docker Compose integration, and Docker Scout (image vulnerability scanning) are polished. Docker Engine itself (daemon only, no GUI) remains free and is the most common production-facing tool in Dockerfiles and CI.
Lima / colima (open source).

Lima is the VM layer that OrbStack, Rancher Desktop, and others build on. colima is a minimal CLI wrapper for Lima that spins up a container runtime with a single command. Popular in CI environments where Docker Desktop is unavailable and a full GUI is unnecessary.

runs.text: The canonical runtime for production Kubernetes (containerd, CRI-O) is now entirely separate from the development toolchain. This decoupling is healthy: local tooling can evolve without affecting cluster runtimes.

The 'post-Docker era' framing is somewhat misleading — Docker the CLI and Dockerfile format are more dominant than ever. What changed: Docker the company no longer controls the production runtime (containerd does), and Docker Desktop no longer has a monopoly on local development. The OCI standard (images, runtimes, registries) is the durable outcome — every tool in this list speaks OCI.

Docker Desktop's paid licensing pushed developers toward alternatives: OrbStack for macOS performance, Rancher Desktop for local K8s, Podman Desktop for rootless containers. Docker Engine itself (and Dockerfiles) remain the standard. The real shift is that OCI images and containerd are the production standard — no single vendor controls the runtime anymore.
